definition: Demure means quiet, modest, and reserved.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word demure. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know demure should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The new hire is demure in meetings — hands folded, questions saved for email — and merciless at the Friday crossword.
Quiet is far milder than demure — it counts decibels and nothing else, and a quiet person may still argue you flat in a whisper; demure adds modesty and composure, chosen on purpose.
Withdrawn goes further than demure — the demure guest is at the table, composed and pleasant; the withdrawn one has left the conversation while still in the chair.

Soft-spoken measures one thing: volume. A soft-spoken person may still run the meeting, argue hard, and hold every eye in the room. Demure covers the whole manner — voice, posture, opinions held back — a composed smallness someone has chosen on purpose.

A retiring person shrinks from notice itself, slipping out of gatherings and dreading introductions. The demure person does not hide: she is present, composed, and pleasant, keeping her own volume low by choice rather than avoiding the room.

Whichever French verb demure came from, its family stayed behind in France — no English relative survives to compare it with. Learn the manner it names directly: quiet, composed, and choosing to be both.
Demure means quiet, modest, and reserved.
The 1908 etiquette manual devotes a full chapter to the demure entrance: eyes level but soft, voice pitched low, opinions offered only when asked twice.
What it teaches is not shyness — the manual is plain that a hostess must never seem afraid of her own parlor — but a chosen smallness of manner, composure worn like a well-cut coat.
Demure is the exact word for that manner, because it means quiet, modest, and reserved — with the calm underneath doing the real work.
A demure person is not hiding or trembling; she has set her own volume low on purpose.
Shy names what someone cannot help; demure names what someone chooses.
neutral / a little old-fashioned
Demure is approving or gently teasing, never harsh, and it mostly describes manner — a demure reply, a demure bow.
Shy is the involuntary cousin; soft-spoken measures only volume.
It is also this unit's quietest impostor: the de- is French furniture, not the prefix, and nothing about a demure person has been lowered — the composure is the whole point.

At twelve, Priya Nair was already the most feared junior player in the state, though nobody watching her between rounds would guess it.
While other competitors paced and boasted, she sat perfectly still, answered questions in a few gentle words, and thanked every opponent, win or lose.
Reporters kept calling her demure, and her coach never corrected them — but he knew the word described a choice, not a lack.
The stillness was a kind of discipline.
Everything she saved by staying modest at the table, she spent on the board.
Opponents who mistook the stillness for meekness rarely made the mistake twice.
